title: Fiduciary Collection Executor for Heirs
one_liner: A service that inventories, appraises and sells inherited card, comic, toy and coin collections for estate lawyers and executors, with an audit trail built for fiduciary liability.
customer: Probate and estate attorneys, trust officers, professional fiduciaries and family executors, billed per estate.
problem: Collections built by boomers and Gen X now carry five- to seven-figure values after record card prices, but heirs have no idea what they hold. 'We buy collections' buyers lowball, and executors are liable if they sell below fair value. Large estates and donations also need qualified appraisals.
solution: Photo-inventory intake (on-site or shipped kit), visual identification and comps, graded-versus-raw triage, sign-off by a qualified appraiser, and sale through the best channel (auction house, game store, streaming seller) under a published fee schedule. The output is an estate-ready valuation report with full custody and sale documentation.
why_now: Card prices are at records ($16.5M for a PSA 10 Pikachu Illustrator, $1.4M for a PSA 9). Visual AI has cut cataloging cost sharply. The wealth transfer is under way.
revenue_model: A flat inventory and appraisal fee ($500-3,000) plus a 10-15% sale commission. Referral relationships with law firms.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the collector but the fiduciary, who carries legal liability. Liability aversion unlocks budget, and the moat is trust artifacts (documented process, appraisal compliance) that any dealer cannot offer because the dealer sits on the other side of the trade.
first_30_days: Give a talk to 15 probate attorneys and 5 fiduciaries in one metro titled 'What is in Grandpa's basement.' Offer a $299 rapid triage, partner with a certified appraiser, and close the first 5 estates.

title: Convert Legacy RPA Bots Using Their Own Logs
one_liner: Use years of bot execution logs as free ground-truth tests to convert brittle RPA bots into monitored agents at a fixed price per bot.
customer: Mid-market companies (500-10,000 employees) with 20-300 UiPath, Blue Prism or Power Automate bots in finance ops, claims and HR, plus RPA consultancies as a channel.
problem: Vendor and consultancy estimates put RPA upkeep at several times license cost, and UI changes break bots constantly. Leaders want agents but fear regression, and migration advice is generic ('retire the brittle ones first'). RPA vendors are pivoting to agentic pitches themselves, which increases pressure without giving a safe method.
solution: Ingest bot definitions and run logs, replay historical inputs to a candidate agent, and differentially test its outputs against the bot's recorded outputs. Cut over each bot when parity passes a threshold, keep the old bot in shadow for 30 days, monitor for drift, and price per bot converted plus a run-and-monitor fee.
why_now: Computer-use agents can operate UIs reliably enough to compete with scripted bots, and RPA vendors are moving to orchestration. Budgets are earmarked because maintenance costs are visible.
revenue_model: $2-$6k per bot conversion plus $200-$500/month per bot run and monitoring, with revenue share for consultancy partners.
non_obvious_insight: The hard part of migrating automations is knowing the new one is right. Legacy bots have already produced years of labeled input-output pairs for free, which turns migration into differential testing.
first_30_days: Find 10 mid-market RPA shops and ask each for 5 brittle bots. Convert 5 bots across 2 customers in shadow mode, show parity, and sign a fixed-fee conversion for the next 20.

title: Phishing Simulations for Agent Approvers
one_liner: Plant known-bad agent actions into human approval queues and prove to auditors and insurers that your reviewers actually catch them.
customer: Heads of finance ops, claims, compliance and internal audit at companies whose agents require human approval (payments, refunds, claims, access requests, code merges), plus cyber underwriters who ask about controls.
problem: Human-in-the-loop is the default answer to agent risk. Step two: volume makes approval a reflex, so the gate decays into a rubber stamp. Step three: regulators and auditors ask for oversight that is demonstrable and measurable (EU AI Act Article 14 and NIST AI RMF language), and no company can show that reviewers catch anything. Injected test cases are recommended in practice writing, but nobody productizes them.
solution: Middleware in the approval path (Slack, Teams, ServiceNow or custom queues) that injects synthetic, internally labeled bad cases at calibrated rates: a vendor bank-detail change, an out-of-policy refund, a prompt-injected request. It measures catch rate and latency by reviewer, queue and time of day, and adapts injection frequency. Output is an oversight effectiveness report with confidence intervals for auditors and insurers, plus queue-design advice (fewer, better gates).
why_now: Agents multiply approval volume. The EU AI Act's human-oversight requirements are still on the books for 2027 and insurers now ask about controls in questionnaires. Approval fatigue is widely acknowledged but unmeasured.
revenue_model: $2-8k/month per approval workflow, or $30-$100k/year enterprise licenses, with an audit-evidence add-on.
non_obvious_insight: KnowBe4 built a large company by testing humans rather than training them. The presence of a reviewer is not a control, but a measured catch rate is, and it doubles as evidence in insurance and audit conversations.
first_30_days: Build for Slack approvals with an accounts-payable bank-change scenario. Run it with 3 finance-ops teams and deliver a first report stating how many planted errors reviewers caught. Use anonymized catch-rate results as the sales asset.

title: Inventory Clearinghouse for Game Stores
one_liner: A store-to-store exchange and standing bid desk that converts hobby shops' slow-moving sealed product into cash or swaps for what customers actually want.
customer: Independent local game stores and card shops (several thousand in the US) that must keep buying broadly to hold their Pokemon and Magic allocation, plus small online breakers who buy sealed at a discount.
problem: The story insiders tell is scarcity: allocation cuts, scalpers, sell-outs. But distributors allocate hot product by account history and volume, so stores end up holding lines they cannot move. Wizards is shipping 7 standard sets in 2026, four of them crossovers (TMNT, Marvel, The Hobbit, Star Trek), and ICv2 reports Pokemon flippers melting down. Cash gets trapped in cold SKUs while the hot ones are short.
solution: A web and SMS app where a store lists overstock (photos, case counts) and sees standing bids from a vetted pool of other stores, breakers and wholesalers. It also finds swaps, such as your Marvel cases for my Pokemon boxes at an index price built from public sold data. We hold payment in escrow, consolidate freight, and guarantee a 72-hour bid on the top ~200 SKUs.
why_now: 2026 has the highest Magic set count ever, and Universes Beyond is now half the calendar. The Pokemon flipper meltdown is compressing secondary margins. Tariffs raised landed costs, so dead stock hurts more. Whatnot's commission change hit existing sellers on 21 Sept 2026, so breakers are hunting cheaper sealed supply.
revenue_model: 3-6% fee on cleared trades, a freight-consolidation margin, and $49/month for bid-desk analytics. Later, short-term working-capital advances against listed inventory.
non_obvious_insight: The same distributor system that starves stores of hot product forces them to carry cold product, and neither distributors nor publishers profit from store-to-store liquidity, so nobody has built it. Stores rarely compete with each other across metros, so they will trade. The clearing spread is the business.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 stores in 2-3 adjacent metros through owner Discords and Facebook groups. Run a manual weekly bid sheet on 30 SKUs using a spreadsheet and Stripe. Spend $30k of your own money on 20 cases of the worst-moving product and resell them to online breakers. First fee revenue by week 3.

title: Microschool Compliance Kit With Built-In Insurance
one_liner: State-by-state registration, safeguarding, ESA and scholarship vendor onboarding, records and liability insurance sold as one subscription to microschool founders.
customer: Microschool founders and learning-pod operators (10-40 students each) and microschool networks; about 1,000 microschools are reportedly in limbo awaiting federal tax-credit rules.
problem: Microschool legal status differs by state, scholarship-credit eligibility rules are unresolved, ESA vendor marketplaces are closed and painful to enter, and insurers are wary of unregulated child programs. Founders are ex-teachers and parents drowning in paperwork, and states are scrutinizing (Pennsylvania cited Alpha School for significant deficiencies).
solution: A compliance operating system: a state legal-status wizard, prefilled filings, fire and occupancy checklists, background-check and mandated-reporter workflows, attendance and records, ESA vendor applications and invoicing, and a bundled liability and abuse-and-molestation policy through an MGA partnership.
why_now: The scholarship credit begins in 2027 in 31 states, ESA programs are expanding (Texas had 200k+ applicants), and the microschool count is growing while final rules are in flux.
revenue_model: $199-399 per month per school SaaS, insurance commission of 15-20% on premiums of about $2-6k per school-year, and a $500 ESA vendor concierge fee.
non_obvious_insight: The moat is not software but insurability. Insurers will price a standardized, audited operating model far better than a random pod, and whoever accumulates loss-ratio data first sets the industry standard.
first_30_days: Pick two ESA states, build checklists and a $750 'launch audit', and sell to 20 founders through microschool founder groups. Pre-negotiate terms with an MGA or broker.

title: Ex-Sales-Rep Route Collectives for Critical-Metal Scrap
angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x waste/circular economy/critical minerals
one_liner: Commission-only teams of laid-off SDRs and inside-sales reps that each own a territory and sign machine shops and dental and electronics labs to take-back programs for tungsten carbide and cobalt scrap. Lots are aggregated and sold directly to domestic reclaimers.
customer: Sellers: tens of thousands of small generators such as machine and tool-and-die shops, carbide grinding shops and dental labs. Buyers: domestic carbide and tungsten reclaimers and refiners that now need US-allocated feedstock. Reps: displaced sales staff.
problem: The BIS rule restricts tungsten scrap exports and the DoD and DOE are subsidizing domestic supply, but supply is scattered across small generators who sell to local yards at a steep discount or trash the hard-to-value streams such as grinding swarf. The bottleneck is sales coverage of the long tail, not recovery technology. Entry-level SDR and BDR roles are among the first white-collar jobs AI is absorbing, leaving a large pool of trained cold-outreach talent.
solution: Each rep owns a metro territory and signs 30-100 shops to a free take-back program: lockable bins, an assay or XRF-based price sheet, payment by lot and simple compliance paperwork (including BIS and toll-processing documentation). Consolidate through partner yards or carriers and sell aggregated lots to reclaimers on term offtake. Start with carbide inserts and grinding swarf, then add cobalt-alloy turnings. Reps keep 15-25% of the net spread and a software backbone handles pricing, pickup scheduling and payouts.
why_now: The BIS allocation rule created a domestic-first buyer set. Machine shops are squeezed by tariffs and input costs and welcome found cash. SDR and entry-level sales roles are being cut in 2026 and reps are actively looking for commission work. The DOE ($134M) and DoD rare-earth and critical-mineral funding raise buyers' willingness to pay for documented domestic feed.
revenue_model: Spread on aggregated lots (buy at a fixed percentage of the reclaimer price and sell at the offtake price). Service fee on compliance paperwork. Later, SaaS for yards and reclaimers.
non_obvious_insight: In critical-material recycling the scarce resource is neither collection technology nor recovery chemistry but sales coverage of thousands of tiny generators. The people best at long-tail coverage are exactly the ones AI has just made cheap.
first_30_days: Pick one machine-shop-dense metro. Get a reclaimer to sign an offtake letter. Recruit five ex-SDRs and have them call 500 shops from public industrial directories. Collect and sell the first few tons of carbide and swarf, and document real price gaps versus the shops' current yards.

title: Data Centers Fund Their Host Utility's Leak Repairs
one_liner: A turnkey program where a data-center developer pays to cut real water losses in the host utility's own system and gets a signed, metered, same-source volume to show regulators and neighbors.
customer: Data-center developers and colo operators fighting permit resistance (Cheyenne, Ohio, New York, Texas), plus the small and mid-size host utilities that receive the repairs. The developer pays.
problem: Insiders think 'water positive' means wetland or agricultural offsets in some other watershed. Locals and regulators now want physical relief on the same source in the same year. Meanwhile many small utilities lose 20-30% of what they treat, and can't fund repairs.
solution: Run an AWWA-style water audit of the host utility. Rank repairs by gallons saved per dollar (main breaks, service leaks, failed valves and meters). Fund local crews and verify the savings with district-metered-area flow data. Deliver a signed 'verified gallons saved' report to both the utility and the permitting file. The utility gets capacity to serve the new load without new supply.
why_now: Texas is making data-center non-reporting a crime and a bar to permits. Ohio scrapped its general discharge permit after more than 7,000 comments, New York has a moratorium, and Cheyenne revoked a permit. Australia's planned standards explicitly cover funding extra water infrastructure. Developers need mitigation that neighbors can verify.
revenue_model: 10-15% program-management fee on repair spend, margin on crew contracts, and a performance bonus per verified 1,000 gallons saved. A $15-25k paid feasibility study is the door-opener.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest same-source gallon is one the utility already treated and lost. This turns the data center from the utility's rival for water into its capital source, and 'water positive' gets judged by neighbors and permitting boards, not by sustainability reports.
first_30_days: Use public loss-audit filings (Texas, Georgia and California require them, in my understanding) to rank utilities near contested or pending data-center projects by real losses per connection. Write a 10-page 'loss-to-offset' report on three of them. Send it to the developers, and to the utilities as a free mailer. Aim for one paid feasibility study within 30 days.

title: Bind-Ready Binder for Florida Condo Boards
one_liner: One package that coordinates inspections, reserve study and appraisal into a carrier-ready submission, then places the master policy.
customer: Florida condo associations (50-300 units, older buildings), their managers and agents.
problem: SB 4D inspections and reserve-study rules mean carriers want documents before they bind a master policy. Special assessments run $50K-$200K+ per unit, and insurance can be 40-60% of the HOA budget (secondary sources, verify). Boards juggle engineers, reserve-study firms, appraisers and agents separately.
solution: An underwriting package that coordinates the milestone inspection, structural reserve study, insurance appraisal and roof and electrical reports. It produces a carrier-ready binder, places it across 10-plus carriers and E&S markets, and re-certifies annually. The binder is the product, and brokerage is the money.
why_now: Florida's market has flipped and carriers are re-entering. Soft reinsurance rewards well-documented risks with better pricing.
revenue_model: $4-9K package fee per association plus placement commission and referral fees from engineers.
non_obvious_insight: In a softening market, underwriting outcomes are decided by document completeness. The board's problem is coordination, not price.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed agency, sign 5 association managers, and build the binder template from 2 real inspections.

title: Farmer-Photo Crop Insurance Verification
one_liner: Replace satellite guesswork with dense, fraud-checked farmer photos, read by locally trained crop models, to trigger insurance payouts.
customer: Agricultural insurers and reinsurers, agri-input companies and cooperatives in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.
problem: Western models fail spectacularly on African crops, index insurance has high basis risk, and manual claim verification costs more than a smallholder premium.
solution: A local crop-damage model trained on image datasets (one project has 5M+ crop images) that takes geo-tagged WhatsApp photos, cross-checks neighbouring farms and weather, and triggers mobile-money payouts. The wedge is one maize or coffee cooperative with one insurer.
why_now: Local crop datasets and small on-device models exist now, and FarmerChat has answered 8M+ farmer questions, so farmers already talk to AI on their phones.
revenue_model: $0.50-2 per policy per season for verification, or a share of premium.
non_obvious_insight: Basis risk is solved by dense ground truth from the insured themselves, not by better satellites.
first_30_days: Partner with a cooperative of about 2,000 farmers and run photo verification in parallel with existing claims for one season.

title: Camera Sentinels for Screwworm on Ranches
one_liner: Solar cameras at water troughs and chutes that flag wounded animals early, so ranchers can act before quarantine.
customer: Texas and Southern cattle ranchers, feedyards and stockyards, plus livestock insurers.
problem: New World screwworm is confirmed in Texas cattle and wound checks on huge pastures are impossible with scarce labor, while one missed case can trigger quarantine and lost sales.
solution: Cellular solar cameras with computer vision fine-tuned on wound and head-shaking images, alerts with geotags, and exportable inspection logs to support movement documentation.
why_now: Confirmed screwworm in Texas, a Mexican feeder-cattle halt removing about 1.2M head a year, and record cattle values make early detection worth real money.
revenue_model: $40-90 per camera per month plus installation, with possible insurer and state-program subsidies.
non_obvious_insight: You are selling regulatory insurance rather than analytics: the asymmetry of one undetected case versus a daily-check labor bill makes even a noisy sentinel valuable.
first_30_days: Install about 20 off-the-shelf trail cameras on five Texas ranches, collect wound imagery with local vets, and run a 30-day alert pilot billed per camera.

title: Proof-of-Resident Public Comment
one_liner: Privacy-preserving verification that a public comment or 311 report comes from a real resident, without collecting their identity.
customer: City clerks, county boards, school districts, planning departments and state agencies running public-comment portals.
problem: Governments use GenAI to write documents, and vendors and activists use AI to flood the channels back. Councils and agencies can no longer tell 50 real residents from 5,000 bot-generated comments, so legitimate voices lose weight and hearings are contested.
solution: A comment widget that accepts a zero-knowledge proof from a mobile driver's license or wallet credential, proving residency and unique personhood without revealing name or address. Public dashboards show verified versus unverified counts, and the clerk keeps an audit log.
why_now: Mobile driver's licenses are live in a growing number of states, and wallet-level zero-knowledge proofs shipped in 2025. The signal-to-noise collapse from AI-generated submissions is now visible in procurement and public comment.
revenue_model: $5-30K per year per jurisdiction, with per-verification fees for state agencies and rulemaking dockets. Partner with agenda-management vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Verification without identity is the only approach that a hostile public will accept. Councils do not want a citizen database, they want a trustworthy count.
first_30_days: Build the widget with an open wallet-credential library in a state that supports mobile IDs. Pilot with one city clerk for a controversial hearing. Publish the verified-versus-unverified result.

title: Affordable Capital-Stack Solver for Conversion Developers
one_liner: A structuring engine and expert memo that tells first-time affordable developers which subsidy stack is fundable for a given office conversion, with a calendar of deadlines.
customer: Office owners, small and mid developers and nonprofits pursuing conversions on public land or under affordability mandates, and city housing agencies running RFPs.
problem: Conversions are moving to public land and affordable set-asides (NYC's 100 Gold Street grew to 4,000 units with 1,000 affordable). That drags market-rate developers into a 6-8 source stack (4% LIHTC and bonds, land lease, abatements, historic credits, PACE, city and state gap funds) with volume-cap timing and set-aside tradeoffs. Consultants charge $25-75K and take months, and deals die before they start.
solution: Input a building and city, and get the top three feasible stacks with set-aside options, equity pricing ranges, application calendar and funder checklists. A human affordable-housing finance specialist reviews each output and delivers a structuring memo; an add-on kit supports public-land RFP responses.
why_now: The 2025 federal tax law eased the bond test for 4% credits and raised 9% allocations starting 2026. Conversions increasingly require affordability, and distressed-office buyers need a plan quickly.
revenue_model: $8-20K flat structuring memo, a 0.5% success fee on closed subsidy, and $1.5K per month developer subscription.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not capital but a first-timer's knowledge of which stack is fundable and when. The winning product is an eligibility-and-calendar engine, not another architect's feasibility study.
first_30_days: Recruit two former affordable-housing finance directors. Publish stack templates for three cities with conversion incentives. Approach 20 office owners and receivers in those cities. Sell three memos at a $6K founder price.

title: Scam Fire Drills: A Security Detail for Grandparents
one_liner: Wealthy families run kidnap and extortion protocols with duress words and a 24/7 first-response team; for $20/mo, give ordinary families rehearsed scam drills and a 15-minute fraud hotline, funded partly by the banks that eat the losses.
customer: Adult children (35-55) with parents 70+, and the credit unions and community banks that sponsor the service for older members. The buyer pays $20/mo per family, or a bank pays $3-6 per enrolled member.
problem: FTC data shows consumers reported $15.9B in fraud losses in 2025, with people 50+ reporting $4.3B and impersonation scams over $3.5B. Awareness campaigns fail because panic overrides knowledge in the moment, and identity-monitoring products act after the money is gone. Recovery windows (wire recalls, gift-card and crypto-ATM freezes, ACH returns) are hours long, and most victims do not know the first-hour steps.
solution: Family onboarding: credit freezes for all members, passkeys and a password manager, SIM-swap locks, a family safe word, and trusted-contact registration at banks. Quarterly consented drills: a scripted call using a synthetic voice (never a relative's cloned voice) tests how the parent responds to a 'grandchild in jail' or 'bank fraud department' scenario, with coaching afterward. A 24/7 hotline answers within 15 minutes with a step-by-step recovery playbook, initiating wire recall, card dispute and gift-card issuer calls while the money can still be clawed back.
why_now: AI voice cloning has made grandparent and executive-impersonation scams cheap, and 2025 losses jumped by a quarter or more from 2024. Credit unions are actively seeking member-protection programs; for example, Illinois law from 1 January 2026 lets credit union staff contact a member's listed trusted person when exploitation is suspected.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family; $3-6 per member per month from credit unions and community banks (reduced fraud losses and liability, and a retention benefit); referral fees on identity-theft insurance and data-broker removal partners.
non_obvious_insight: Rehearsal, not awareness, changes behavior under panic, exactly as fire drills do; nobody sells consented scam simulations to families. The first-hour response is where dollars are actually saved, so a human hotline is the product, and the party with the strongest incentive to pay is the financial institution that absorbs the loss.
first_30_days: Recruit 20 families through parent-of-aging-parents communities and run a manual onboarding call plus one drill each with a contract fraud analyst on call. Record the drill failure rate as a headline stat. Pitch two local credit unions on a 100-member sponsored pilot, priced at $4 per member per month.

title: Repatriation-of-Remains Concierge for Immigrant Families
one_liner: A fixed-price service that gets a loved one's body home across borders, and later a low-cost membership that pre-funds it.
customer: Immigrant families on one corridor at a time (for example US to Mexico or Central America, the Philippines, India or Nigeria), plus consulates, churches, mosques, community associations and funeral homes without international skills.
problem: Sending remains home costs thousands (often $5-15K, unverified) and requires consular paperwork, health permits, embalming, sealed caskets, air cargo rules and destination-side logistics. Families use GoFundMe, church collections and opaque middlemen, in days, while grieving.
solution: Intake in the family's language, document assembly (consulate forms, permits), a vetted network of embalmers, cargo forwarders and destination funeral homes, insurance and payment plans, and one coordinator. Later add a $8-$15/month repatriation membership underwritten through a licensed insurer partner.
why_now: Community payment and remittance rails are digital, translation and document assembly are cheap with AI, and immigrant communities are large and trust-network driven. Funeral homes treat this as an add-on they don't understand.
revenue_model: 15-25% service margin on $6-12K cases, membership fees, and insurer commissions.
non_obvious_insight: The mainstream industry treats repatriation as a sideline, but for these families it is the primary product. Corridor-specific know-how is the moat, and trust travels through churches and consulates.
first_30_days: Choose one corridor and one metro. Partner with a funeral home that already does it. Sign 3 churches or a consulate liaison. Run 5 cases at cost to document the exact process and price it.

title: Original-Recording Music for Memory Care
angle: Pairing 1: Aging & silver economy x Creator economy / AI provenance
one_liner: A playlist and licensing service for memory-care communities that matches each resident's favorites to the exact original master, and flags re-records, sound-alikes and AI covers that streaming catalogs are now full of.
customer: Memory-care and assisted-living operators (activity directors), adult day centers, home-care agencies and board-certified music therapists. Adult children pay for a family tier.
problem: Personalized music is one of the few low-cost tools that reaches people with dementia, but it depends on recognition of a specific, familiar recording. Streaming catalogs are riddled with 'greatest hits, re-recorded' versions, sound-alike compilations and now AI tracks. Deezer says over 50% of daily uploads are fully AI, and Sony has asked for 135,000+ impersonations to be removed. Understaffed activity directors cannot tell a 1966 master from a 2019 re-record, and facilities also carry public-performance licensing exposure.
solution: Intake asks a resident or family for songs, era, and where they danced or heard it. The software resolves each song to the original ISRC and audio fingerprint of the label master, rejects re-records, covers and AI-flagged tracks, and produces a device-ready playlist with the public-performance license bundled. Families can add human-made voice messages and personal recordings, stamped as verified human. Staff get a one-page 'response log' to note which tracks got reactions.
why_now: AI-track volume passed human uploads on Deezer in July 2026. Spotify, TIDAL and Bandcamp now label, demonetize or ban AI music, so machine-readable authenticity signals exist for the first time. Memory-care occupancy sits near a record 90%, the 80+ population is growing fast, and blood-test diagnosis pushes more families into post-diagnosis coping tools.
revenue_model: $99-199 a month per community, $12 a month for a family tier, and a per-seat licensing bundle where labels or collecting societies agree to a senior-living rate. Later, a B2B API for music therapists.
non_obvious_insight: In this setting the active ingredient is the exact recording rather than the song, and that is a provenance problem. The 'AI flood' harms the most vulnerable listeners because it degrades the catalog a caregiver assumes is authentic. The first pilot should test the hypothesis that covers and re-records underperform originals.
first_30_days: Build a resolver on public metadata (MusicBrainz, Discogs, label catalogs) and a fingerprint service. Offer a free 'playlist audit' to 10 memory-care communities and to Music & Memory-certified programs. Track staff-logged resident responses for original versus re-record and publish the result as your credibility asset.

title: Widowhood Risk Program Sold to Medicare Payers
one_liner: Use hospice's early knowledge that a caregiver spouse is about to become a widow to enroll them in a 180-day protective program, paid for by Medicare Advantage plans and ACOs.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans (especially those with dual-eligible special needs plans), ACOs and value-based primary care groups. Hospice agencies are the intake channel and receive a referral or administrative fee.
problem: The spouse of a hospice patient is the second patient, and nobody is paid to treat them. The caregiver spouse ran the pillbox, the checkbook, the driving and the meals. They have skipped their own appointments for months. In the weeks after the funeral their chronic conditions decompensate, and hospitalizations, ED visits and falls spike. The chaplain is the one person who sees the untouched pills, the empty refrigerator and the missed doctor visits. Payers only learn of the death through enrollment data that lags by weeks or months. Hospice bereavement services are a mailing program, and they do not bill for the spouse's medical risk.
solution: A two-part program. Before the death, a hospice chaplain or social worker flags a high-risk caregiver spouse using a 6-item checklist (medication management ownership, driving, isolation, own chronic conditions, missed visits) and refers them, with consent, to the program. After the death, a community health worker does a home visit within 72 hours, books a primary care appointment within 14 days, does a medication reconciliation, sets up meal delivery and transport, and runs structured check-ins at 2 weeks, 6 weeks and 6 months. The 6-week and 6-month checks include a prolonged grief screen (PG-13-R). Screen-positive people are referred to therapists trained in prolonged grief disorder treatment, billable to insurance because PGD has had its own diagnosis code (F43.81) since October 2022.
why_now: Medicare Advantage margins are under pressure, and plans are hunting for measurable avoidable-utilization programs and star-rating improvements. Value-based primary care and ACOs are expanding, and both are rewarded for preventing ED visits and admissions. Prolonged grief disorder became an official DSM-5-TR diagnosis in 2022, with an ICD-10-CM code from October 2022, so the treatment side is finally billable. Hospices are being asked to show quality beyond death itself. I could not verify current bereavement benefit designs at specific plans, so check that before pitching.
revenue_model: A per-enrolled-spouse fee of about $150 to $300 per month for 6 months, paid by the plan or ACO. This can convert to shared savings once there are a few hundred enrollees. Hospices receive a per-referral fee or a bereavement-outsourcing fee. Therapy referrals bill insurance directly, and the program can hold a small clinician panel. Employer benefit teams are a later channel.
non_obvious_insight: The highest-risk patient is not on the payer's radar and is not the patient the hospice is paid to look after. Only the hospice team knows the caregiver is fading, and it knows months before any claim or enrollment record does. The widowhood effect (well documented in the research literature, with elevated mortality and hospitalization in the months after a spouse dies) is an underpriced, predictable utilization event.
first_30_days: Pick one regional hospice and one value-based primary care group or small MA plan with a few thousand lives. Build the checklist and a simple spreadsheet workflow, then hire one community health worker or licensed social worker. Enroll the first 20 spouses at no charge, tracking ED visits, missed PCP visits and grief screens at 90 and 180 days. Use the data to sell a paid pilot to the plan or group before month 6. Get a HIPAA lawyer to sign off on the referral pathway and consent language.

title: Vaults After Banks
one_liner: Buy or lease closed bank branches with intact vaults and reopen them as private safe-deposit clubs for the people banks are abandoning.
customer: Crypto self-custodians storing seed-phrase backups, families doing estate planning, small collectors and small businesses. Referral channels are estate attorneys and financial advisors. Boxes run $150-900/yr.
problem: Big banks are exiting safe-deposit service. JPMorgan is reported to be leaving the business, and Santander and Capital One have stopped new boxes. Large boxes have multi-year waitlists in cities. Storing seed phrases or a will at home is risky, and a bank box has a known weakness: heirs can't get in without a court process.
solution: Acquire or lease shuttered branches whose UL-rated vaults and box banks are already installed. Sunk-cost vaults are nearly worthless to a seller and costly to build new. Add modern access control (biometrics plus dual-key, video, private viewing booths) and insurance. Build a strong KYC and lawful-process program from day one, without inventorying box contents. Then differentiate with a sealed 'Legacy Envelope': tamper-evident, chain-of-custody logged, and released to named heirs through an attorney-verified protocol. Add a notary and witness room for signing estate documents on site.
why_now: Bank exits are accelerating through 2025-26, and branch closures keep feeding the market with sale-ready vault buildings. Self-custodied crypto has gone mainstream, and holders are worried about physical coercion. Independent operators like BlueVault report growing demand, so the model is proven but far from saturated outside a few metros.
revenue_model: Annual box rent ($120-900 by size). One-time onboarding fee. Legacy Envelope release plans ($60/yr plus $250 on release). Hourly notary and witness room. Attorney and advisor referral fees. A 1,500-box vault at about 70% fill and $300 average is roughly $315k/yr against a building that can cost $250-500k.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is trust and the legal chain of custody after death, not the steel. Banks leave because a box earns little against corporate overhead, but a one-branch boutique with a lawyer-drafted custody agreement is profitable. The US Private Vaults FBI seizure in 2021 shows the failure mode, so the winning brand is 'privacy plus compliance', never 'no questions asked'.
first_30_days: Pull 20 recently closed branches from LoopNet and bank real-estate-owned lists and shortlist the ones with intact vaults and box banks. Get a vault-contractor inspection and an insurance quote. Have a lawyer draft the custody agreement and Legacy Envelope protocol. Open a waitlist with $100 refundable founding-member deposits, targeting 300 members through crypto meetups and estate-attorney networks before signing a lease.

title: Diaspora-Financed Home Batteries for Family Back Home
angle: Pairing 2: Energy transition & grid x Emerging markets leapfrogging
one_liner: Sell home battery and solar systems to migrants in the US, UK, Canada and EU as a monthly subscription that keeps the lights on for their relatives, underwritten on the sender's credit rather than the recipient's.
customer: Diaspora professionals (Nigerian, Ghanaian, Kenyan, Filipino, Nepali, Bangladeshi) who already fund fuel, diesel and generator repairs for relatives, with installers in the origin city as fulfilment partners.
problem: Families in Lagos, Accra, Nairobi or Manila face daily outages and spend remittance money on diesel and petrol for generators. Local households are unbankable for asset finance, USD lenders carry FX and default risk, and pay-as-you-go schemes collect tiny local-currency payments. The Hormuz shock has raised fuel costs and put about $50bn of Gulf remittances at risk.
solution: A subscription sold in USD, GBP or CAD. A vetted local installer fits a 5 kWh LFP battery plus hybrid inverter (and optional panels) at the relative's home, the sender pays by card over 24-36 months, and ownership transfers at the end. Underwriting uses the sender's developed-market credit profile. A shared app shows the sender live uptime and savings, and the family gets a simple power ledger. On default, the fallback is remote throttling or redeployment of the unit.
why_now: Stationary battery prices fell 45% in a year and Africa already imports more battery dollars than panels. Felix shows migrant payments can run over chat apps at $8B scale. The US 1% tax on cash-funded remittances pushes senders toward card-funded rails (buying goods and services delivered abroad is not a remittance transfer, subject to legal review), and Nigeria and Kenya are opening rules for digital-dollar settlement.
revenue_model: Hardware margin of 15-25% plus a financing spread (about 18-25% effective APR), installer referral fees, and insurance and extended-warranty attach. Dollar collections match dollar-denominated hardware and DFI debt, removing the FX mismatch.
non_obvious_insight: Credit risk is being priced on the wrong person. The one who effectively pays for the outage today is the diaspora sender, through diesel money, and that person has a credit file, a card and hard-currency income. The caregiving motive should also produce lower churn than pay-as-you-go.
first_30_days: Put up a landing page taking $500 refundable deposits through 3-5 Nigerian, Ghanaian or Kenyan diaspora WhatsApp, church and alumni groups. Contract one Lagos or Nairobi installer and ship 20 systems. Use uptime screenshots and family videos for the referral flywheel, and fund working capital from deposits plus a small angel or DFI debt line.

title: Inherited-Rental Stabilization Service for Estate Attorneys
one_liner: A flat-fee 30-day service that stabilizes rental properties the moment an owner dies, sold through probate attorneys and trust officers who fear personal liability.
customer: Probate and trust-and-estates attorneys, professional fiduciaries and bank trust departments who represent executors and heirs of deceased small landlords. Attorney or fiduciary pays the flat fee out of the estate. Beneficiaries later pay ongoing management or sale-prep fees.
problem: The average small landlord is in their 60s or older, and a wave of these owners is dying and passing on 2-to-30-unit portfolios to heirs who have never landlorded. In the first 60 to 90 days after death everything degrades. Tenants get confused about who to pay and some quietly stop, so collections drop 20 to 40%. The named insured on the policy is dead and coverage gets contested or non-renewed. Security deposits, a legal liability that has to be accounted for in trust, are mingled into the deceased's personal account. Leases are undocumented handshake month-to-months, and vendors stop being paid. The attorney does not want to run a rental business but is exposed to a beneficiary surcharge claim if value leaks.
solution: A productized 'Day-1 Stabilization Package' delivered by a small field team and software. It has five parts. First, a tenant estoppel and 'pay here' notice with a new rent-collection account, sent within 5 days. Second, a rent-roll and lease audit, verifying every tenant, deposit and lease term against bank records. Third, deposit-liability reconciliation and a segregated trust account. Fourth, insurance re-papering: new named-insured and vacancy status filings. Fifth, a code-compliance and deferred-maintenance walk-through, with photos, for the estate inventory and stepped-up-basis appraisal support. The output is a court-ready fiduciary report the attorney can file. The last step is an option: convert to ongoing management at a preferential rate, or a sale-ready package for listing.
why_now: The great wealth transfer from boomers is reaching real estate now, and small individual landlords are among the oldest owner cohorts. Rising property values make each estate's rental portfolio high-stakes. Attorneys are reluctant to run operating businesses, and fiduciary surcharge risk is well understood. Large PM firms ignore 6-unit estates. Cloud rent collection and e-sign tools make a 30-day remote-plus-local process feasible for a tiny team.
revenue_model: $2,500 to $6,000 flat fee per estate (scaled by unit count), paid by the estate. About 30 to 40% of estates convert into ongoing management at 7 to 9% of rent, or into a listing or sale referral with a 1 to 2% fee. Bank trust departments can be sold an annual retainer.
non_obvious_insight: The best property-management clients are never won through marketing. They arrive through a death, and the person deciding who gets the call is an attorney who cares about liability, not price or software features. The attorney's real product need is documentation to defend against beneficiary surcharge claims, not better rent collection. The real revenue leak in the first 90 days is the 'ghost landlord' period, when tenants do not know who to pay.
first_30_days: Write the checklist and notice templates (a weekend of work if you have PM experience). Contact 30 probate attorneys and 5 corporate fiduciary or trust officers in one metro, offering a free 45-minute CLE-style talk on 'the first 90 days of an inherited rental portfolio' through the county bar's trusts and estates section. Offer a discounted first stabilization at cost to two attorneys for testimonials and case studies. Line up a bookkeeper and a local handyman for the field-work side and use existing PM software for rent collection.

title: Turnkey Recovery Amenity Operator for Landlords
one_liner: Operate managed sauna-and-cold-plunge suites inside apartment and mixed-use buildings, paid a flat monthly fee by the landlord.
customer: Owners and operators of multifamily, mixed-use and office buildings with underused fitness rooms and an amenity-arms-race problem.
problem: Insiders treat recovery as a consumer studio business (one brand went from zero to 25 contrast-therapy studios in about 20 months and plans 100 more), with retail rent, foot-traffic marketing and wet/hot-room liability. Meanwhile landlords already own the square footage and want differentiators, but cannot operate saunas and plunge tubs (cleaning, water treatment, safety, insurance).
solution: Design, install (modular saunas and tubs) and operate a recovery suite: booking app, resident access control, daily cleaning and water testing, camera-free safety monitoring, waiver and insurance management. The landlord pays a flat monthly operating fee; residents can pay small fees for guests or premium hours.
why_now: Nordic-style social wellness attendance grew about 33 percent in 2025, sauna and cold-plunge hardware is a $1B+ market and getting cheaper, and HSA-linked home sauna sales show pre-tax demand exists even without a studio.
revenue_model: $3-8k per month per property operating fee (or revenue share above a threshold) plus $40-120k build-out margin.
non_obvious_insight: The best customer for the sauna boom is not the Gen Z consumer but the landlord: acquisition cost is one sales call instead of a marketing budget, and what the landlord is really buying is zero-liability operation, not wellness.
first_30_days: Cold-outreach 100 mid-size multifamily owners in one metro with underused amenity rooms, then pilot one building with a rented modular sauna and a $3k plunge tub on a 90-day contract at about $2.5k per month while tracking resident usage and renewal intent.
